tier_reason: First-party charts in BENCHMARKS.md (.github/benchmarks/*.png) from the public harness HappySeaFox/sail-benchmark (src/sail-benchmark-sail.cpp, src/sail-benchmark-stb.cpp, run-benchmarks.sh) with MSVC 2019 and an i7-4800MQ stated, but the page gives no flags (the harness README only says CMake Release), the charts date from 2021-11-06 with an unpinned vcpkg library set and a harness that has changed since, and the category incumbents (libjpeg-turbo, libpng) are never measured directly, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: JPEG YCbCr 6000x4016 (microseconds, chart labels): SAIL 226,067 vs stb_image 351,115 (1.55x faster, derived from page data), OpenImageIO 262,450, CImg 251,370, Boost.GIL 265,826, FreeImage 237,112, SDL_image 229,923; level with DevIL 226,361 and about 8% slower than WIC 209,636. Other JPEG YCbCr sizes: 1000x669 SAIL 4,577 vs stb_image 7,842 (1.71x, derived from page data); 15000x10040 SAIL 632,004 vs stb_image 1,190,281 (1.88x, derived from page data), DevIL 625,547 slightly faster; 100x67 SAIL 103 vs stb_image 138 (fastest of nine). JPEG Gray 6000x4016: SAIL 72,449 vs stb_image 103,020 (1.42x), SDL_image 114,930, OpenImageIO 83,176; level with FreeImage 72,756, DevIL 72,261 and WIC 70,683; at 15000x10040 SAIL 370,049 vs stb_image 518,181 (1.40x) but behind FreeImage 355,372, WIC 356,068 and DevIL 367,734. PNG: stb_image beats SAIL on every PNG chart: PNG RGBA 6000x4256 SAIL 515,651 vs stb_image 334,286 (stb 1.54x faster) and WIC 348,043, ahead of OpenImageIO 647,908 and CImg 584,293; PNG RGBA 100x71 246 vs 198, 1000x709 10,633 vs 8,234, 15000x10640 3,187,903 vs 1,993,125; PNG Gray 6000x4256 SAIL 142,685 vs stb_image 97,276 (stb 1.47x faster) and WIC 103,314; PNG Gray 15000x10640 900,536 vs 558,613.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2019 x64; the harness README builds with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and --config Release (MSVC Release defaults, no explicit flags stated on the benchmark page); all libraries including SAIL installed from vcpkg with no pinned versions (vcpkg.json has no baseline); Google Benchmark, mean of 5 repetitions per image (run-benchmarks.sh)
corrections.caveats: SAIL's JPEG and PNG codecs are libjpeg-turbo and libpng (README codec table), and its times sit within about 1-2% of DevIL, SDL_image and FreeImage, which wrap the same codecs; the win over stb_image is therefore libjpeg-turbo's win over stb_image's JPEG decoder, not something SAIL adds, and libjpeg-turbo is already a verified wave 10 entry. The category incumbents (libjpeg-turbo, libpng) are never benchmarked directly. stb_image is faster than SAIL on every PNG chart (1.24x to 1.60x) and WIC beats it on large PNGs. 'Default pixels' means each library returns its own default pixel format, so the work done can differ between libraries. The charts were last regenerated on 2021-11-06 (SAIL commit aa55083 'SAIL: Update benchmarks') with a pre-1.0 SAIL (the harness log names sail-0.9.0-pre14 for the May 2021 run) on a Windows 7 laptop with a 2013-era Core i7-4800MQ; the harness has changed since (the DevIL target is commented out in the current CMakeLists.txt although DevIL is in the charts, sail-benchmark-sail.cpp was edited in November 2023, vcpkg updated in January 2026) and vcpkg.json pins no versions, so the published numbers cannot be reproduced from current sources. Numbers are chart-image labels; BENCHMARKS.md has no text numbers. The harness also covers gdk-pixbuf, GraphicsMagick and OpenCV, which are absent from the published charts. The seed URL (sigrok.org/wiki/Libsigrok) is not SAIL; the awesome-c entry is mislinked, so the record was matched by its description to HappySeaFox/sail.

notes: All quoted chart numbers match the PNG charts (I read 12 of the 16, including all 6000-wide ones); tier C stands. SAIL is a multi-format wrapper whose JPEG/PNG speed is libjpeg-turbo's and libpng's (already-verified wave 10 libjpeg-turbo), so the orchestrator may prefer decision duplicate under the wrapper rule (precedents sharp, net-vips, jpeg4py); otherwise keep with shortcomings: off-category baseline (stb_image), slower than stb_image on all PNG charts, 2021 charts from an unpinned and since-changed harness. Metadata checked: MIT, 359 stars, 29 forks, last commit 2026-09-12 ('SAIL: Bump to 1.3.0'), not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: The only numbers are search snippets of a blocked Arm Community blog post (June 2024, retelling a 2023 Fraunhofer HHI study, 'over 200% performance gains' for VVenC/VVdeC ported to Neon with SIMDe) and of arXiv 2309.16509 (1.51x to 5.13x over original SIMDe); no hardware, compiler, flags or harness could be read, and the SIMDe repo and wiki carry no benchmark, so C (snippet only) at best.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the Arm Community blog post 'Porting to Arm Intrinsics with SIMDe Part 1' (developer.arm.com, published 2024-06-26 per search snippet; EGRESS_BLOCKED here), its source study 'Open and optimized VVC Implementations on ARM Architectures' (Bross, Lehmann, Hege, Wieckowski, Fraunhofer HHI, 2023; abstract in CEUR-WS Vol-3562 SEViC23-abstract5, EGRESS_BLOCKED), the FOSDEM 2024 VVdeC-on-Arm slides (EGRESS_BLOCKED) and arXiv 2309.16509 (EGRESS_BLOCKED) could not be opened, so hardware, compiler flags, per-workload breakdown and the exact baseline are unverified; my snippets say 'over 200% performance gains' without naming the baseline, the earlier search agent's snippet said over unvectorized code. The baseline is the program's own scalar fallback, not one of the category baselines (std::valarray, std::transform, std::reduce, <cmath>), and the gain is that of SIMD vectorization rather than of SIMDe over another SIMD route; SIMDe's translation has overhead versus hand-written Neon (the AWS Graviton SIMD guide advises rewriting hot paths in native Neon after a SIMDe port, and Fraunhofer later hand-optimized VVdeC with arm_neon.h). The arXiv paper's baseline is SIMDe itself (RVV-enhanced vs original SIMDe on XNNPACK). On x86 with native intrinsics SIMDe should simply match them. The SIMDe README, wiki and repo have no benchmark numbers or benchmark directory. Needs a second pass from a thread that can open developer.arm.com, ceur-ws.org and arxiv.org.

notes: Tier C kept on snippet-only evidence (Arm blog URL found via search and set as benchmark_url, but EGRESS_BLOCKED, as were the CEUR-WS abstract, FOSDEM slides and ar5iv/arXiv); if the orchestrator wants the strict null-page rule, it is D. Shortcomings: snippet-only numbers, baseline is scalar fallback code outside the category list, the speedup is SIMD over scalar rather than SIMDe over an alternative, and SIMDe has overhead versus hand-written Neon. Metadata checked: MIT (COPYING is the MIT text), 3.1k stars, 323 forks, last commit 2026-09-30, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: README benchmark tables compare directly against std::vector with public harness code (test/bench/solo.cpp driven by scripts/bench/render_charts.py, one container per process, median of 9), and state gcc 16.1.1, -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG, boost 1.90.0, abseil 20260107.1 and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X pinned with taskset.

corrections.caveats: The win over std::vector is concentrated in workloads that stay inside the inline storage (std::vector must allocate) and in std::string element work; on pure bookkeeping with trivially copyable elements svector loses to std::vector (push_back 2.2x slower, subscript about 18% slower, swap slower) and loses to absl::InlinedVector at filling inline storage (0.48 ns per element). Several differences are inside the stated run-to-run spread (under 3%, about 6-7% for std::string workloads): the bolded emplace_back std::string win (22.64 vs 23.52 ns, 3.9%) and the insert-at-front std::string win (1320.2 vs 1415.2 ns, 6.7%) are within or at the edge of that spread even though the README bolds them; only build-7-inline (3.1x) and shuffle+sort (12%) clearly exceed it. The last commit date is a dependabot bump; the last functional commit is 2026-08-05. libstdc++ is implied by gcc (test/bench/solo.cpp comments refer to libstdc++ string swapping), not stated as a version. Young container maintained by one person.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README tables and the harness (test/bench/solo.cpp) looks sound: every workload keeps its result alive with doNotOptimizeAway and the build_inline workload sums the elements to stop the optimizer deleting inline vectors. Shortcomings: wins only in inline-storage and std::string workloads, slower than std::vector on push_back (2.2x), subscript (18%) and swap; two of the bolded wins are within the stated noise.
